summary: Systems paper on serving many concurrent coding agents: KV-cache offloading to CPU memory only pays if the host tier holds the 'reuse working set' of all active agents. EfficientAgent estimates that working set with a stack-distance model, sizes the host tier accordingly, and adds a write-admission rule to LMCache/vLLM that declines refills only when the tier is too small. Evaluated by replaying OpenHands + Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B SWE-bench Verified trajectories on H20, RTX 3090 and H800 GPUs.

claims.claim: Sizing the host tier to the estimated working set cuts recomputed prompt tokens by 93% and end-to-end time by 39%.
claims.evidence: §5.2 / Fig. 2: computed prefill 76.7M -> 5.3M tokens (93.1%) and makespan 209 -> 128 min (38.7%) going from 5 to 20 GiB per rank on 8xH20. Note this is a capacity increase (5 -> 20 GiB), not the admission algorithm; the comparison is within one replayed workload.

claims.claim: Write admission cuts recomputation by 35% with a small tier and avoids the 4.3x penalty of always filtering with a large tier.
claims.evidence: §5.5: at 5 GiB conditioned admission 76.7M -> 49.7M computed prefill (35%), makespan 208.9 -> 187.1 min; at 40 GiB fixed admission raises prefill 5.3M -> 22.8M (4.3x), conditioned admission stays at 5.3M.

claims.claim: Stack-distance model predicted the capacity transition before the experiments.
claims.evidence: §5.4 / Tables 4-5: predicted 5.19-5.78M computed prefill at 20 GiB and 5.19-5.31M at 80 GiB; measured 5.28M and 5.29M. At 10 GiB the model under-predicted recovery (55.3-58.9M predicted vs 65.2M restored). Pre-registration of predictions is asserted, not externally timestamped.

claims.claim: Offloading pays only on GPUs with low compute per host-link byte.
claims.evidence: Table 1: RTX 3090 offload/recompute 0.91 (dense 0.92), H20 0.60 when tier ≥ working set, H800 1.08-1.87 across all configs. Three GPU types, two models.

patterns.note: Argues context-management (folding, pruning, summarization) should be judged by the cache-stable prefix it preserves: an early rewrite rekeys every later KV chunk. 98.1% of prompt tokens in a call were already processed in the prior call.
Quantifies token cost structure of agent loops (each task submits 1.86M prompt tokens, 80x its output) and gives KV memory sizing formulas; no budget caps.
Concurrency (active pool of 8 vs 16 agents) changes serving cost: halving the pool cut makespan 24.8% under recomputation.

methodology.sample: One recorded live SWE-bench Verified run replayed: 4,427 model calls, 147.1M prompt tokens; host capacities 3-80 GiB/rank; active pool 8 and 16; 17 replay runs at A=16.
methodology.baselines: vLLM GPU prefix caching (recompute), unmodified LMCache offload, fixed write admission. Current, appropriate baselines; other agent-aware serving systems (Continuum, KVFlow, etc.) discussed but not run.
methodology.models: Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct (MoE) and Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct (dense, subset of deployments).
methodology.variance: A few independent repeats (two recompute runs agree to 0.2%; two 40 GiB offload runs 123.7/124.0 min); most points single runs, but replay is deterministic in tokens.
methodology.ablations: Fixed vs conditioned admission across capacities; concurrency; GPU memory fraction sweep; parameter sensitivity (App. D).
methodology.contamination_controls: n/a (serving performance, task quality not the claim).
methodology.languages: SWE-bench Verified (Python repos); language irrelevant to the serving claim.

standards.artifacts: Code, replay framework and stack-distance analysis tools at https://github.com/KunmingSHAO/efficientagent_release; full configs in App. A, every run in App. B.
standards.preregistration: Authors state stack-distance predictions were recorded before running specific capacity points (§5.4); no external registration.

biases.detail: All policy comparisons replay one OpenHands/CodeActAgent trajectory set on SWE-bench Verified; other harnesses with different context growth patterns (e.g. compaction) could shift the working set.
Abstract's '93% / 39%' headline comes from quadrupling host memory, not from the proposed admission policy, whose gain is 35% recomputation / ~10% makespan at 5 GiB.
Authors' own admission policy and replay methodology evaluated by the authors; mitigated by released tools and deterministic replay.

verdict_reason: Numbers in the abstract appear exactly in §5 with deterministic replay and released tooling, so the systems claims are solid; relevance to a team using hosted agent hosts is low, and the headline gain is from more host memory rather than the new policy.
applicability: Only relevant if the team self-hosts open-weight models for agents (e.g. for data residency). Then: size CPU KV tiers by (concurrent agents x context length), and expect offloading to hurt on high-FLOP GPUs. For hosted agent hosts (Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, Hermes) the transferable lesson is about prompt-cache economics: harness features that rewrite early context (summarizing compaction, reordering rules files, injecting dynamic content at the top) invalidate provider prefix caches, so keep stable content (AGENTS.md, specs for the several repositories) at the front and append-only. No bearing on Java, spec-driven development, or cross-repository work logic.
